extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged British public, members of Parliament, and informed readers concerned with constitutional government and ministerial responsibility
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical standards for judging the constitution, selection, and conduct of executive ministers and the role of Parliament in a constitutional monarchy. Focuses on how administrations should reflect the legislature and public opinion, and on institutional means to prevent faction and abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration correspondent to its legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Every sort of government ought to have its administration correspondent to its legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If administration does not correspond to the legislature, 'things must fall into an hideous disorder.' In a free commonwealth the executory system should not be composed of persons on whom the people have no dependence; ministers must be acceptable to the people because the very being of the state depends on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive operation of political institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every good political institution must have a preventive operation as well as a remedial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions ought to have a natural tendency to exclude bad men from government rather than trusting the safety of the state to subsequent punishment, which has ever been tardy and uncertain and may fall on the injured rather than the criminal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular election of magistrates and disposition of honors
rubrics_metrics.description: The popular election of magistrates, and popular disposition of rewards and honors, is one of the first advantages of a free state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without such popular influence (or something equivalent) a people cannot long enjoy the substance of freedom or the vivifying energy of good government. The constitution may provide for the effects of popular election without the mischiefs of perpetual canvass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament's duty to refuse support until ministers acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: It had always been held the first duty of Parliament to refuse to support government, until power was in the hands of persons who were acceptable to the people, or while factions predominated in the court in which the nation had no confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This negative power secured the good effects of popular election without the mischiefs of continual popular canvassing; the loss of this power would mean the loss of Parliament's effective control and reverence with the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should have prior public estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before men are put forward into the great trusts of the state, they ought by their conduct to have obtained such a degree of estimation in their country as may be some sort of pledge and security to the public that they will not abuse those trusts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper use of power is secured when a man has shown by the general tenor of his actions that the affection, good opinion, and confidence of his fellow-citizens have been among the principal objects of his life; appointments should not reward persons whose importance began with office and will end with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude knots or cabals without public principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Those knots or cabals of men who have got together, avowedly without any public principle, in order to sell their conjunct iniquity ... ought never to be suffered to domineer in the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such groups are odious and have no connection with the sentiments and opinions of the people; they should be prevented from taking positions that confer the lead and direction of public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid administration disposed by one man's uncontrolled pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of government which has left its whole executory system to be disposed of agreeably to the uncontrolled pleasure of any one man ... is a plan of polity defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trusting appointments to the mere will of a sovereign (however virtuous) is consequentially erroneous in every part of the constitution; executive appointments must be constrained by constitutional mechanisms and public dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the 'double cabinet' / interior cabinet scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'double cabinet' or an 'interior cabinet' that separates administration from the court and divides authority brings the whole body of government into confusion and contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a scheme produces foreign-policy weakness, inconsistency in colonial administration, loss of authenticity in official correspondence, and general impotency; it makes ministers shadows with no ultimate disposal of affairs and destroys coherent counsel and execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration must have energy and capacity to execute
rubrics_metrics.description: A system that benumbs and stupefies the whole executive power renders government languid, uncertain, ineffective; making ministers fearful of attempting, and incapable of executing any useful plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good administration must combine security of freedom with vivifying energy; it should not produce neither the security of a free government nor the energy of an absolute monarchy but should enable decisive, consistent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid militarization and hired mobs as remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Fierce licentiousness begets violent restraints; the military arm is the sole reliance ... The civil power, like every other that calls in the aid of an ally stronger than itself, perishes by the assistance it receives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the military or hiring mobs to manage domestic disorder undermines civil authority, encourages licentiousness, and produces anarchy without freedom or servitude without submission; constitutional and preventive measures are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Commons as a control for the people (not upon them)
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons was designed as a control for the people; its virtue, spirit, and essence consist in being the express image of the feelings of the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should bear the stamp of the actual disposition of the people, show sympathy with constituents, and not be a permanent standing government detached from public sentiment; otherwise it ceases to be a House of Commons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of Commons: vigilance, care of public money, openness
rubrics_metrics.description: A vigilant and jealous eye over executory and judicial magistracy; an anxious care of public money; an openness, approaching towards facility, to public complaint: these seem to be the true characteristics of a House of Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than acting as an instrument to support peace and subordination, the Commons should monitor administration, guard the treasury, and be approachable to public grievance to ensure trusteeship for the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: The public's opinion must remain a means of power
rubrics_metrics.description: If the opinion of the country be of no use as a means of power or consideration, the qualities which usually procure that opinion will be no longer cultivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing popular incentives turns ambition toward the court and away from country service; the people must retain influence so that public-spirited qualities are fostered and government remains accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointments should avoid degrading the sovereign's dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The system of favoritism has tended to degrade the personal dignity of the sovereign, exposing him to contradictions and mortifications by compelling compliance with measures contrary to the people's affections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sovereign's private ease and dignity are impaired when appointments are made to secure court faction rather than public esteem; true friends to the crown are not mere sycophants created by office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons should be transitory and reflect popular disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons was supposed originally to be no part of the standing government ... It was considered as a control issuing immediately from the people, and speedily to be resolved into the mass from whence it arose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transitory nature and middle character between subject and government are essential; the Commons must remain closely connected to popular feelings rather than becoming a permanent detached institution.
